intro: A Bloom filter can reject unseen items without storing every key. Collisions can produce false positives, so membership means possibly present rather than definitely present.
task: Set membership bits and construct an example where a never-inserted query still receives a positive answer.
requirements: insert_hashes and query_hashes are integer-valued matrices (N,K) and (M,K), sharing positive K. size is an integer 1..100000; every hash index lies in [0,size-1].
Set each inserted bucket in a boolean bit vector. A query is possibly present only if all its buckets are set.
Return dict bits as a length-size boolean NumPy vector and maybe_present as a length-M boolean vector. There is no deletion, counter array, or false-positive probability estimate.

Numeric inputs must be real and finite with magnitude at most 1e30, except where a stricter bound is stated. Booleans are not numeric parameters. Leave all caller inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

examples.name: A false positive from combined bits

hints.title: Insertion is a bitwise OR operation
hints.body: Repeated inserts do not change a bit after it becomes true.

hints.title: A query requires every bit
hints.body: One unset bit proves absence; all set bits only suggest membership.

explanation: Bloom filters have no false negatives for correctly inserted items under a fixed hash mapping, but different items can collectively set all bits needed by a query.
The worked false-positive example separates the membership guarantee from exact storage. A positive result should trigger a definitive lookup when correctness requires certainty.
